description: DNS resolution decomposed. Client → stub resolver → recursive resolver → root → TLD → authoritative server. Caching at every level. Resource record types (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, SOA, CAA). Modern variants: DoH (over HTTPS), DoT (over TLS), DoQ (over QUIC). DNSSEC adds cryptographic signatures. The Internet's most-used lookup system, fundamental to nearly every connection.

sub_mechanisms.name: stub_resolver
sub_mechanisms.definition: Client-side DNS library (in OS: getaddrinfo). Forwards queries to a recursive resolver; doesn't walk the hierarchy itself.
sub_mechanisms.why: Per-process DNS code would be heavy. OS-provided stub resolver caches + handles retries. Programs do gethostbyname or getaddrinfo and get IP back.

sub_mechanisms.name: recursive_resolver
sub_mechanisms.definition: Resolver that walks the DNS hierarchy: queries root, then TLD, then authoritative — recursively. Caches results.
sub_mechanisms.why: Centralised resolution amortises hierarchy traversal across many clients. ISP runs one for its customers; public ones (8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1) serve everyone. Caching is the resolver's value-add: ms latency vs hundreds.

sub_mechanisms.name: root_servers
sub_mechanisms.definition: 13 named root servers (a.root-servers.net through m). Hundreds of physical instances via anycast. Top of the DNS hierarchy.
sub_mechanisms.why: Bootstrap of the hierarchy. Recursive resolvers know the root server IPs from configuration. Roots delegate to TLDs (.com, .org, .uk). Anycast lets each query reach the closest root instance.

sub_mechanisms.name: TLD_servers
sub_mechanisms.definition: Top-Level Domain servers: .com is run by Verisign; .org by Public Interest Registry; country TLDs by national registries.
sub_mechanisms.why: Below root in the hierarchy. TLD servers delegate to authoritative servers for individual domains. The TLD operator is responsible for the namespace's integrity (e.g., Verisign's role in .com security).

sub_mechanisms.name: authoritative_server
sub_mechanisms.definition: DNS server hosting the actual records for a domain. example.com's records live on its authoritative servers (named in NS records).
sub_mechanisms.why: Domain owners control these. Cloudflare, AWS Route53, Google Cloud DNS are popular hosted authoritative providers. Authoritative ≠ recursive: roles are separate.

sub_mechanisms.name: resource_record_types
sub_mechanisms.definition: A (IPv4 address), AAAA (IPv6 address), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), NS (nameserver), SOA (start of authority), TXT (arbitrary text), CAA (which CAs may issue certs).
sub_mechanisms.why: DNS isn't just hostname → IP. Each record type carries different information. TXT is the universal extension point (SPF, DKIM, domain ownership verification). CAA was added for certificate security.

sub_mechanisms.name: TTL_caching_lifetime
sub_mechanisms.definition: Each record carries a TTL (seconds). Resolvers cache it for that duration. After expiry, fresh lookup required.
sub_mechanisms.why: Tradeoff: short TTL = fast change propagation but more load; long TTL = less load but slow propagation. CDNs often use 60-300 sec TTLs. Migrations require lowering TTL in advance.

sub_mechanisms.name: DNS_over_UDP
sub_mechanisms.definition: Default: queries sent over UDP, port 53. Single packet request, single packet response.
sub_mechanisms.why: Lightweight: no TCP setup overhead. Limited to ~512 bytes original spec; EDNS0 extends to ~4096. Beyond that, retry over TCP. Most queries fit in UDP.

sub_mechanisms.name: DNS_over_TCP
sub_mechanisms.definition: Fallback when UDP response would be too large or when zone transfers are needed.
sub_mechanisms.why: Zone transfers (AXFR/IXFR) require TCP for reliability + ordering. Large responses (many records) exceed UDP size. TCP fallback indicated by truncated UDP response's TC bit.

sub_mechanisms.name: DNSSEC_signatures
sub_mechanisms.definition: Cryptographically signed DNS records. RRSIG signature accompanies each record set. Chain of trust via DS records up to the signed root.
sub_mechanisms.why: Authenticates DNS responses against tampering / spoofing. Recursive resolvers validate signatures; clients trust the validation. Adoption ~25% of domains; deployment friction has been operational complexity.

sub_mechanisms.name: EDNS0_extension
sub_mechanisms.definition: Extensions to DNS allowing larger UDP responses (4096 bytes), client subnet hints, DNSSEC OK flag.
sub_mechanisms.why: Original DNS's 512-byte limit constrained modern use (DNSSEC signatures are large). EDNS0 negotiates larger size. Client subnet (ECS) lets CDNs return location-appropriate responses for client subnets (controversial for privacy).

sub_mechanisms.name: DoH_DNS_over_HTTPS
sub_mechanisms.definition: RFC 8484. DNS queries inside HTTPS requests, port 443. Indistinguishable from web traffic.
sub_mechanisms.why: Privacy from ISP. Bypasses ISP-level DNS hijacking / censorship. Centralisation concern: many users default to one DoH provider (Cloudflare, Google) — single point of observation.

sub_mechanisms.name: DNS_cache_poisoning
sub_mechanisms.definition: Injecting forged responses into a resolver's cache. Classic attack: race the legitimate response with a forged one matching the transaction ID.
sub_mechanisms.why: Pre-mitigation (random source port + 0x20 randomisation), the 16-bit transaction ID was guessable. Kaminsky's 2008 attack made this practical. Modern mitigations + DNSSEC raise the bar.

derivation_rules.name: hierarchy_enables_distributed_authority
if: names are organised hierarchically with delegation
then: each level can be managed independently
derivation_rules.why: Verisign manages .com; Cloudflare manages cloudflare.com under .com; etc. No central authority controls all names. Delegation lets each domain owner control their subdomain without affecting others. Distributed scalable authority.

derivation_rules.name: caching_amortises_hierarchy_traversal
derivation_rules.why: Cold lookup: walks the hierarchy (4+ round-trips). Cached lookup: instant. Real-world DNS load is dominated by cached hits. The TTL mechanism is what makes caching effective + correct (cache invalidation by expiry).

derivation_rules.name: DNSSEC_authenticates_against_spoofing
then: forged responses are detectable and rejected
derivation_rules.why: Signatures bind responses to the legitimate authoritative server. An attacker can inject forged responses, but without the signing key, they can't produce a valid signature. Validating resolvers reject invalid responses.

derivation_rules.name: DoH_provides_query_privacy
then: network observers see only that DNS over HTTPS is happening, not the queries themselves
derivation_rules.why: TLS encrypts query content. ISP sees TCP/443 connection but not the domain queried. Major privacy improvement. Centralisation trade-off: the DoH provider sees all queries.

derivation_rules.name: low_TTL_for_dynamic_records
derivation_rules.why: Cache freshness vs lookup load tradeoff. CDNs use short TTLs (~60s) to enable failover; static records (your MX server's IPv4) use long TTLs (86400s). Application choice based on change rate.
